query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin aluminide coating to equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will enhance its oxygen resistance by promoting the formation of a coherent, protective alumina (Al2O3) scale without compromising its established room‐ and high–temperature mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic, as-cast HfNbTaTiZr that shows 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strengths of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹ but suffers from inadequate oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin aluminide coating (via methods such as pack cementation or physical vapor deposition) on the surface of the alloy.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at high temperatures (around 800 °C) for at least 5 hours, with the requirement that both room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength remain preserved.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a uniform, adherent Al2O3 scale at the coating/alloy interface that acts as an oxygen diffusion barrier.
generation.mechanism: Upon exposure to high-temperature oxidizing environments, the aluminide coating preferentially oxidizes to form a slow-growing and protective Al2O3 layer. This dense scale prevents further oxygen ingress and pesting while the underlying alloy retains its microstructure and mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated alloy will exhibit significantly reduced oxidation rates and pesting, with preserved tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength compared to the uncoated material.
generation.baseline: Uncoated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits inadequate oxygen resistance resulting in pesting under high-temperature air exposure.
generation.boundary: The intervention is applicable under high-temperature (≈800 °C) conditions in oxidizing atmospheres and must be optimized so that the coating’s thickness and processing do not alter the intrinsic mechanical properties of the bulk alloy.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal coating thickness, deposition parameters, and long-term scale stability need further investigation. It is also uncertain how slight Al diffusion might affect the near-surface microstructure over extended service periods.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples: one with the thin aluminide coating and one without. Expose both sets to air at 800 °C for 5 hours. After exposure, analyze surface oxidation, oxide scale adherence, and residual mechanical properties.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and composition (using SEM, EDS, and XRD)
Room-temperature tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength (via mechanical testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminide-coated samples do not exhibit significantly improved oxidation resistance (e.g., similar oxide scale thickness, weight gain, or evidence of pesting) or if their mechanical properties (ductility or yield strength) are degraded relative to the uncoated samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

Oxidation Behavior of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 High-Entropy Alloy Powder

Abstract: One of the most promising applications of FeNiCoCrMoAl-based high-entropy alloy is the fabrication of protective coatings. In this work, gas-atomized powder of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 composition was deposited via high-velocity oxygen fuel spraying. It was shown that in-flight oxidation of the powder influences the coating’s phase composition and properties. Powder oxidation and phase transformations were studied under HVOF deposition, and during continuous heating and prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. Optical and scanning electron microscopy observation, energy dispersive X-ray analysis, X-ray diffraction analysis, thermogravimetric analysis, differential thermal analysis, and microhardness tests were used for study. In a gas-atomized state, the powder consisted of BCC supersaturated solid solution. The high rate of heating and cooling and high oxygen concentration during spraying led to oxidation development prior to decomposition of the supersaturated solid solution. Effect of Al Addition on Microstructure and Properties of CoCrNi Medium-Entropy Alloy Prepared by Powder Metallurgy

Abstract: AbstractPowder metallurgy possesses the advantages of low energy consumption, less material consumption, uniform composition, and near-final forming. In order to improve the mechanical properties and high-temperature oxidation resistance of CoCrNi medium-entropy alloy (MEA), CoCrNiAlX (X = 0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7) MEAs were prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) and spark-plasma sintering (SPS). The effect of aluminum content on the microstructure and properties of the MEAs was investigated. The results show that the CoCrNi MEA is composed of face center cubic (fcc) phase and some carbides (Cr23C6). With the increase in Al content, there exists Al2O3 precipitation. When the Al content is increased to Al0.5 and Al0.7, the body center cubic (bcc) phase begins to precipitate. The addition of aluminum significantly enhances the properties of the alloys, especially those containing fcc+bcc dual-phase solid solutions.
